title: AP Physics 1: Algebra-Based
summary: Practise motion, force, energy, momentum, rotation, oscillations and fluids.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the current eight-unit framework, including fluids in Unit 8. These models do not replace experimental investigations.

modules.title: Position, velocity and constant acceleration
modules.focus: Read a motion model with a chosen positive direction.
explanation: Displacement is final position minus initial position; distance counts the total path length. Average velocity divides displacement by elapsed time. Choose a positive direction before assigning signs so that opposite motion is represented consistently.

For constant acceleration, v=v₀+at and Δx=v₀t+at²/2. These equations are not valid with a changing acceleration unless applied in intervals where the assumption holds. On a velocity-time graph, signed area gives displacement.

workedExample.prompt: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Find velocity and displacement.
steps: Final velocity is 2+3(4)=14 m/s.
Displacement is 2(4)+3(4²)/2=32 m.

misconception.claim: Negative velocity always means negative acceleration.
misconception.correction: Velocity gives direction of motion; acceleration gives change of velocity.

questions.prompt: A runner moves 30 m east then 10 m west in 10 s. Find average velocity east-positive.
An object at rest accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Find displacement.

questions.hint: Acceleration uses final minus initial velocity.
questions.prompt: A cart slows uniformly from +10 m/s to +4 m/s in 3 s. Find acceleration and displacement.
questions.answer: Acceleration is −2 m/s²; displacement is [(10+4)/2]×3=21 m.
checkpoints: Divide by 3 s to obtain −2 m/s².
Use average velocity 7 m/s to obtain 21 m.
hints: Acceleration uses final minus initial velocity.
For constant acceleration, average the endpoints.

questions.hint: Distinguish the slope of position from the slope of velocity.
questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upwards. Ignore air resistance. At its highest point, are velocity and acceleration both zero? Use upward as positive.
questions.answer: Velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration remains −g because gravity still acts; velocity then becomes negative.
checkpoints: Connect the acceleration to the subsequent reversal.
hints: Distinguish the slope of position from the slope of velocity.
The gravitational force remains present at the top.

notes.title: Reasoning through position, velocity and constant acceleration
paragraphs: A motion graph encodes different quantities through height, slope and area. The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity, while the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration. Signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement; distance instead adds the magnitudes of the positive and negative areas. Choose one positive direction and keep it throughout the calculation. Constant-acceleration equations apply only over intervals where acceleration is constant. An object can have negative velocity and positive acceleration: it then moves in the negative direction while its speed initially decreases.

workedExamples.prompt: A cart has velocity −6 m/s and constant acceleration +2 m/s² for 4 s. Find displacement and distance.
steps: It reverses at t=3 s. Displacement is (−6)(4)+(1/2)(2)(4²)=−8 m.
The first triangle of the velocity graph has area magnitude 9 m; the last has 1 m. Distance is 10 m.
workedExamples.conclusion: Displacement is −8 m; distance travelled is 10 m.

flashcards.front: What is the slope of x against t?
flashcards.back: Velocity.

flashcards.front: What is signed area under v against t?
flashcards.back: Displacement.

flashcards.front: When can distance exceed displacement magnitude?
flashcards.back: When direction reverses.

flashcards.front: Does positive acceleration always mean speeding up?
flashcards.back: No; it can reduce a negative velocity magnitude.

modules.title: Free-body diagrams and net force
modules.focus: Sum interactions acting on one chosen object.
explanation: A free-body diagram includes forces exerted on the selected object, not the forces it exerts on other objects. Newton’s second law relates the vector sum of those forces to ma. Zero net force means constant velocity, which can be nonzero.

Newton’s third-law partners act on different objects and therefore do not cancel within one object’s force sum. Circular motion requires inward net force; it is provided by physical interactions such as tension or gravity, not an additional force called centripetal force.

workedExample.prompt: A 4 kg cart experiences 18 N right and 6 N left. Find acceleration.
steps: Choose right-positive and sum forces: 18-6=12 N.
Use a=Fnet/m=12/4=3 m/s² right.

misconception.claim: Third-law force pairs cancel on the same free-body diagram.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass moves in a circle of radius 3 m at 6 m/s. Find inward net force.
A book rests on a table. Are its weight and normal force a third-law pair?
questions.hint: Identify the object each force acts on.
questions.answer: No. Both act on the book; their third-law partners act on Earth and the table.
checkpoints: Pair forces across two interacting objects.
Distinguish equilibrium from a third-law pair.

questions.hint: Velocity direction changes around the circle.
questions.prompt: A 2 kg object moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at 4 m/s. Find the inward net force.
hints: Velocity direction changes around the circle.
Use the radius and squared speed.

questions.hint: Upward acceleration requires upward net force.
questions.prompt: An elevator accelerates upwards at 2 m/s² carrying a 60 kg person. Use g=10 m/s². Find the floor force on the person.
checkpoints: Draw weight and normal force on the person.
hints: Upward acceleration requires upward net force.
The normal force must exceed the weight.

notes.title: Reasoning through free-body diagrams and net force
paragraphs: A free-body diagram contains forces exerted on one selected object. Do not include the forces that object exerts on other bodies, and do not add a separate force labelled motion. Resolve forces along useful axes before applying ΣF=ma. A normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and need not equal weight when other forces or acceleration have perpendicular components. Newton’s third-law partners act on different objects, whereas forces that balance in one free-body diagram act on the same object. Circular motion requires an inward net force assembled from actual interactions.

workedExamples.prompt: A 5 kg crate is pulled horizontally with 30 N against 10 N friction on a level floor. Use g=10 m/s². Find acceleration and normal force.
steps: Horizontal net force is 30−10=20 N, so a=20/5=4 m/s².
Vertical acceleration is zero, so N−mg=0 and N=50 N.
workedExamples.conclusion: The crate accelerates at 4 m/s² horizontally and the normal force is 50 N.

flashcards.front: What belongs on one free-body diagram?
flashcards.back: Forces acting on the selected object.

flashcards.front: Do third-law partners cancel on one object?
flashcards.back: No; they act on different objects.

flashcards.front: Is centripetal force an additional interaction?
flashcards.back: No; it names the inward net force.

flashcards.front: When is N=mg on a horizontal surface?
flashcards.back: When vertical acceleration and other vertical force components are zero.

modules.title: Work and kinetic energy
explanation: For a constant force, work is Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Net work changes kinetic energy. A force perpendicular to motion does no work even though it can change the direction of velocity.

Energy conservation is applied to a defined system. Friction may convert mechanical energy to thermal energy rather than destroy total energy. Power measures the rate of energy transfer and is expressed in watts, equivalent to joules per second.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg cart initially at rest receives 16 J of net work. Find final speed.
steps: Net work equals ΔK, so 16=(1/2)(2)v².
Thus v²=16 and v=4 m/s.

misconception.claim: Energy lost from motion has disappeared.
misconception.correction: It may have transferred to thermal, sound or other energy within a larger system.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force parallel to motion acts over 3 m. Find work.
A device transfers 600 J in 4 s. Find average power.

questions.hint: Only the force component along displacement transfers energy by work.
questions.prompt: A 20 N force acts at 60° to a 4 m displacement. Find its work.
hints: Only the force component along displacement transfers energy by work.
Multiply that component by 4 m.

questions.hint: The forces have equal parallel magnitudes and opposite directions.
questions.prompt: Two equal and opposite horizontal forces each act on a moving cart. Over 3 m one does +15 J. What work does the other do, and what happens to kinetic energy?
questions.answer: The other does −15 J. Their net work is zero, so the cart’s kinetic energy is unchanged if these are the only forces doing work.
checkpoints: Sum the two works to zero.
Apply the work-energy theorem with the stated assumption.
hints: The forces have equal parallel magnitudes and opposite directions.
Kinetic energy responds to net work.

notes.title: Reasoning through work and kinetic energy
paragraphs: Work measures energy transferred by a force through displacement, using the component parallel to that displacement. Net work changes kinetic energy. Potential energy is a system quantity that lets conservative interactions such as gravity or an ideal spring be accounted for without calculating their work separately. Choose one accounting method and avoid counting the same interaction both as external work and as a potential-energy change. Friction can convert organised mechanical energy into thermal energy. A zero net work result establishes unchanged speed between endpoints, but does not imply every individual force did zero work.

workedExamples.prompt: A 3 kg object drops 2 m from rest. Air resistance transfers 12 J to thermal energy. Use g=10 m/s². Find its final speed.
steps: Gravitational potential energy decreases by mgh=3×10×2=60 J; 48 J remains as kinetic energy.
Set (1/2)(3)v²=48, so v²=32 and v≈5.66 m/s.
workedExamples.conclusion: The final speed is approximately 5.7 m/s.

flashcards.front: Which force component does work?
flashcards.back: The component parallel to displacement.

flashcards.front: What does net work equal?
flashcards.back: Change in kinetic energy.

flashcards.front: Can friction conserve total energy?
flashcards.back: Yes; mechanical energy can become thermal energy.

flashcards.front: What is average power?
flashcards.back: Energy transferred divided by elapsed time.

modules.title: Impulse and a sticking collision
modules.focus: Conserve momentum only for an appropriate system.
explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity and is a vector. Impulse equals the change in momentum and is the signed area under a force-time graph. A small average force acting longer can produce the same impulse as a larger force acting briefly.

Total momentum is conserved when the external impulse on the selected system is negligible. In a sticking collision, kinetic energy usually decreases even though system momentum is conserved. Include both colliding objects and retain velocity directions.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. Find their common speed.
steps: Initial momentum is 2(3)+1(0)=6 kg m/s.
The combined mass is 3 kg, so final velocity is 6/3=2 m/s in the initial direction.

misconception.claim: Momentum conservation means kinetic energy is always conserved.
misconception.correction: Kinetic energy can be converted internally in an inelastic collision.

questions.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball changes velocity from +4 to -2 m/s. Find impulse.
A constant 12 N net force acts for 0.25 s. Find momentum change.
questions.answer: 3 kg m/s in the force direction.
checkpoints: Recognise N s equals kg m/s.

questions.hint: Use area, not peak force times duration.
questions.prompt: A triangular net-force pulse rises from zero to 20 N and returns to zero over 0.40 s. Find impulse and velocity change for a 2 kg cart.
questions.answer: Impulse is (1/2)(0.40)(20)=4 N s; Δv=4/2=2 m/s in the force direction.
checkpoints: Divide by mass to obtain 2 m/s.
hints: Use area, not peak force times duration.
Impulse equals mass times velocity change.

questions.hint: A reversal changes momentum even when speed is unchanged.
questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball changes velocity from +5 to −5 m/s over 0.10 s. Find average net force.
questions.answer: Δp=0.20(−5−5)=−2 kg m/s; average force is −2/0.10=−20 N.
hints: A reversal changes momentum even when speed is unchanged.
Divide the momentum change by contact time.

notes.title: Reasoning through impulse and a sticking collision
paragraphs: Momentum is a signed vector quantity, so choose the system and positive direction before using conservation. Internal forces exchange momentum between members but cancel in the system’s total force balance. Total momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible during the interval, even if kinetic energy decreases. Impulse is the area under a force-time graph and equals momentum change; the same change delivered over a longer time has a smaller average force. In an inelastic collision, missing kinetic energy is transformed into deformation, sound or thermal energy rather than disappearing from total energy.

workedExamples.prompt: A 1 kg cart at +6 m/s sticks to a 2 kg cart at −1 m/s. Find common velocity and kinetic energy lost.
steps: Initial momentum is 6−2=4 kg m/s, so the 3 kg combination moves at +4/3 m/s.
Initial kinetic energy is 18+1=19 J; final energy is (1/2)(3)(4/3)²=8/3 J, so loss is 49/3 J.
workedExamples.conclusion: Common velocity is +1.33 m/s and about 16.3 J becomes other energy forms.

flashcards.front: What condition supports momentum conservation?
flashcards.back: Negligible external impulse on the chosen system.

flashcards.front: What is impulse graphically?
flashcards.back: Signed area under force versus time.

flashcards.front: Is kinetic energy conserved when carts stick?
flashcards.back: Generally no.

flashcards.front: How does longer stopping time affect average force for the same impulse?
flashcards.back: Its magnitude decreases.

modules.title: Torque and angular acceleration
modules.focus: Measure force effectiveness about an axis.
explanation: Torque magnitude is rF sin θ, using the angle between the position vector from the axis and the force. A force through the axis has zero lever arm. Specify an axis and a positive rotation direction before adding torques.

For fixed-axis rotation with constant moment of inertia, net torque equals Iα. Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution as well as total mass. Moving the same mass farther from an axis increases its contribution mr².

workedExample.prompt: A perpendicular 8 N force acts 0.5 m from an axle. If I=2 kg m², find angular acceleration.
steps: Torque is rF=0.5(8)=4 N m.
Angular acceleration is τ/I=4/2=2 rad/s².

misconception.claim: Torque depends only on force magnitude.
misconception.correction: Distance from the axis and force direction also matter.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force acts along a line through the rotation axis. Find torque.
checkpoints: A large force can still have zero torque.

questions.prompt: A point mass moves from radius r to 2r about the same axis. How does its inertia change?
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large.

questions.prompt: A wheel has I=0.50 kg m² and experiences torques +3 N m and −1 N m. Find angular acceleration.
questions.answer: Net torque is +2 N m, so α=2/0.50=+4 rad/s².
hints: Find net torque first.
Apply τnet=Iα.

questions.prompt: Two 1 kg masses lie 0.20 m and 0.40 m from an axis. Treat them as particles. Find total inertia and the fraction from the outer mass.
questions.answer: I=1(0.20²)+1(0.40²)=0.20 kg m². The outer mass contributes 0.16/0.20=80%.
hints: Square each distance separately.
Compare 0.16 with the total.

notes.title: Reasoning through torque and angular acceleration
paragraphs: Torque measures a force’s tendency to change rotation about a chosen axis. Its magnitude is force multiplied by perpendicular lever arm, or rF sinθ. The sign depends on the chosen rotational direction. Forces applied farther from an axle can create more torque, but the body’s moment of inertia also matters for angular acceleration. Moment of inertia depends on both total mass and its distance distribution about that axis. For a fixed axis and constant inertia, net torque equals Iα. Translational balance and rotational balance are separate requirements for static equilibrium.

workedExamples.prompt: A horizontal light beam pivots at its centre. A 12 N downward force acts 0.50 m left of the pivot. What downward force 0.30 m right balances it?
steps: The left force produces counterclockwise torque 12×0.50=6 N m.
The right force must produce 6 N m clockwise, so F=6/0.30=20 N.
workedExamples.conclusion: A 20 N downward force at the right point balances the torque.

flashcards.front: What is the lever arm?
flashcards.back: Perpendicular distance from axis to force line of action.

flashcards.front: What makes torque zero?
flashcards.back: A force whose line of action passes through the axis.

flashcards.front: What determines inertia about an axis?
flashcards.back: Mass and its squared distances from that axis.

flashcards.front: What are both conditions for static equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Zero net force and zero net torque.

modules.title: Angular momentum and rolling energy
explanation: Angular momentum about a fixed axis is Iω for a rigid body in that rotation model. It is conserved when net external torque about the chosen axis is zero. Changing I can therefore change ω without an external torque.

Rolling without slipping combines centre-of-mass translation with rotation and satisfies v=ωR. Total kinetic energy is mv²/2+Iω²/2. Rotational energy must be included when relating a rolling object’s height loss to its speed.

workedExample.prompt: A rotating student reduces moment of inertia from 4 to 2 kg m² while external torque is negligible. Initial angular speed is 3 rad/s. Find final speed.
steps: Initial angular momentum is 4(3)=12 kg m²/s.
Set 2ωf=12 to obtain ωf=6 rad/s.

misconception.claim: Conserving angular momentum always conserves rotational kinetic energy.
misconception.correction: Internal work can change kinetic energy while angular momentum stays constant.

questions.prompt: A wheel rolls without slipping at 6 m/s with radius 0.3 m. Find ω.
For I=2 kg m² and ω=4 rad/s, find rotational kinetic energy.
A ring has I=mR² and rolls at speed v. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
questions.answer: Rotational energy is (1/2)mR²(v/R)²=(1/2)mv², equal to translational energy, so the fraction is one half.
checkpoints: Show the two energies are equal.
hints: Express both energies using v.
Compare one term with their sum.

questions.prompt: A rotating system halves its inertia with negligible external torque. By what factor do angular speed and rotational energy change?
questions.answer: Angular speed doubles. Since K=L²/(2I) with L fixed, rotational kinetic energy also doubles; internal work supplies the increase.
checkpoints: Use Iω conservation to double speed.
Identify internal work as the energy source.
hints: Keep angular momentum fixed.
Substitute the new inertia and speed into rotational energy.

notes.title: Reasoning through angular momentum and rolling energy
paragraphs: Angular momentum conservation requires negligible external torque about the specified axis. If inertia changes, angular speed can change even while angular momentum stays fixed; rotational kinetic energy need not stay fixed because internal work can transfer energy. Rolling without slipping links translation and rotation through vcm=ωR. Its kinetic energy contains both centre-of-mass motion and rotation about the centre of mass. For ideal rolling on a stationary surface, the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so static friction can enforce the constraint without doing net work at that contact. Real rolling losses require additional modelling.

workedExamples.prompt: A solid cylinder of mass 2 kg and radius 0.50 m rolls without slipping at 3 m/s. Use I=(1/2)mR². Find total kinetic energy.
steps: Its angular speed is ω=3/0.50=6 rad/s and I=0.25 kg m².
Translational energy is 9 J and rotational energy is (1/2)(0.25)(36)=4.5 J.

flashcards.front: When is angular momentum conserved?
flashcards.back: When external torque is negligible about the selected axis.

flashcards.front: What is the no-slip rolling relation?
flashcards.back: vcm=ωR.

flashcards.front: Does constant angular momentum guarantee constant kinetic energy?
flashcards.back: No; changing inertia can involve internal work.

flashcards.front: What are the two parts of rolling kinetic energy?
flashcards.back: Centre-of-mass translation and rotation about the centre.

modules.title: Spring oscillations and restoring force
explanation: An ideal horizontal spring-mass oscillator obeys F=-kx about equilibrium. The minus sign means force opposes displacement, not necessarily velocity. For mass m, angular frequency is √(k/m) and period is 2π√(m/k).

Total mechanical energy is kA²/2 in the ideal undamped model. Speed is greatest at equilibrium, while spring potential energy is greatest at the turning points. Increasing amplitude changes energy but not the period of this ideal linear oscillator.

workedExample.prompt: A 1 kg mass on a 16 N/m spring oscillates ideally. Find angular frequency and period.

misconception.claim: The restoring force is largest at equilibrium.
misconception.correction: Spring displacement and restoring force are zero there; speed is largest.

questions.prompt: If mass quadruples with the same spring constant, how does period change?
For k=100 N/m and amplitude 0.20 m, find total oscillator energy.
A spring oscillator has k=25 N/m and m=1 kg. At x=+0.08 m, find force and acceleration.
hints: Hooke’s law opposes displacement.
Divide force by mass.

questions.prompt: An ideal oscillator’s amplitude triples without changing m or k. Compare period, maximum speed and energy.
questions.answer: Period is unchanged; maximum speed triples; total energy increases by a factor of nine.
checkpoints: Use period dependence on m/k only.
hints: Separate amplitude from angular frequency.
Track linear and squared amplitude factors.

notes.title: Reasoning through spring oscillations and restoring force
paragraphs: Simple harmonic motion arises when the net restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and points towards equilibrium. For an ideal mass-spring system, ω²=k/m and a=−ω²x. Displacement, velocity and acceleration are not largest at the same point: speed is greatest at equilibrium, while acceleration magnitude is greatest at either extreme. The total mechanical energy is fixed in the undamped ideal model and alternates between kinetic and spring potential energy. Increasing amplitude raises energy and maximum speed but does not change the period while the spring remains in its linear range.

workedExamples.prompt: A 0.50 kg mass on a 32 N/m spring has amplitude 0.10 m. Find maximum speed and acceleration magnitude at an endpoint.
steps: At x=±A, |a|=ω²A=64×0.10=6.4 m/s², directed towards equilibrium.
workedExamples.conclusion: Maximum speed is 0.80 m/s; endpoint acceleration magnitude is 6.4 m/s².

flashcards.front: Where is spring-oscillator speed largest?
flashcards.back: At equilibrium.

flashcards.front: Where is acceleration magnitude largest?
flashcards.back: At the displacement extremes.

flashcards.front: How does doubling amplitude change ideal energy?
flashcards.back: It quadruples energy.

flashcards.front: What does the minus sign in a=−ω²x mean?
flashcards.back: Acceleration points towards equilibrium.

modules.title: Pressure, buoyancy and fluid continuity
modules.focus: Use depth and displaced volume with clear assumptions.
explanation: In a stationary fluid of uniform density, pressure increases with depth by ρgh. Pressure is force per area; it is not itself a force. The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, not automatically the weight of the object.

For steady incompressible flow through a full pipe, A₁v₁=A₂v₂. A narrower section therefore has greater flow speed when volumetric flow is unchanged. Bernoulli’s relation additionally assumes a suitable streamline and negligible viscous losses.

workedExample.prompt: A fully submerged object displaces 0.003 m³ of water. Use ρ=1,000 kg/m³ and g=10 m/s². Find buoyant force.
steps: Displaced water mass is ρV=3 kg.
Its weight, and hence buoyant force, is 30 N upward.

misconception.claim: Every submerged object has buoyant force equal to its own weight.
misconception.correction: Equality occurs in vertical force balance; displaced fluid determines buoyancy.

questions.prompt: Find gauge pressure 2 m below water’s surface using ρ=1,000 and g=10 in SI units.
A pipe’s area halves in steady incompressible flow. What happens to speed?

questions.hint: The same volume crosses each section each second.
questions.prompt: Water flows through a 0.004 m² section at 2 m/s, then a 0.001 m² section. Find volume flow rate and second speed.
questions.answer: Flow rate is 0.004×2=0.008 m³/s; second speed is 0.008/0.001=8 m/s.
hints: The same volume crosses each section each second.
Divide the flow rate by the smaller area.

questions.prompt: An object of volume 0.002 m³ has gravitational weight 30 N and is fully submerged in water. Use water density 1000 kg/m³ and g=10 m/s². What additional upward support force holds it at rest?
questions.answer: Buoyant force is 20 N, so an additional upward support force of 10 N balances the 30 N weight.
hints: Buoyancy depends on displaced volume.
Subtract buoyancy from weight.

notes.title: Reasoning through pressure, buoyancy and fluid continuity
paragraphs: Fluid pressure acts in all directions, while the net buoyant force comes from pressure increasing with depth. The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, not necessarily the object’s weight; they are equal only when vertical forces balance appropriately, such as free floating at rest. Gauge pressure excludes atmospheric pressure. For steady incompressible flow, volume conservation gives A₁v₁=A₂v₂. Bernoulli’s relation additionally assumes an appropriate ideal-flow model; viscosity, pumps and dissipative losses need separate terms. A narrow section can increase speed without increasing the volume flow rate.

workedExamples.prompt: A 600 kg/m³ block floats in water of density 1000 kg/m³. Find the fraction of its volume submerged.
steps: At rest, buoyancy balances weight: ρwater gVsub=ρblock gVtotal.
Cancel g and divide by ρwater Vtotal to obtain Vsub/Vtotal=600/1000=0.60.
workedExamples.conclusion: 60% of the block’s volume is submerged.

flashcards.front: What does buoyant force equal?
flashcards.back: Weight of displaced fluid.

flashcards.front: What is gauge pressure?
flashcards.back: Pressure measured relative to atmospheric pressure.

flashcards.front: What does Av represent?
flashcards.back: Volume flow rate.

flashcards.front: When does buoyancy equal an object’s weight?
flashcards.back: When its vertical force balance requires it, such as free floating at rest.
